input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a widely used and highly effective separation technique, and in this particular case it is applied to the recovery of acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The design is based on a cascade of 8 countercurrent stages, a configuration that is generally considered capable of delivering strong separation performance. A key parameter in this process is the distribution coefficient, which describes how the acetic acid divides itself between the two liquid phases at equilibrium; here, the coefficient takes a value of 1.02 at 25 °C, indicating a slight preference for the organic phase. On the basis of these figures, the predicted recovery is an impressive 95% of the acetic acid present in the feed, underscoring the potential of the staged countercurrent arrangement. It is important to note, however, that this prediction rests on certain idealisations: it assumes that every stage reaches equilibrium, and it assumes that mutual solubility between the two solvents is negligible. Interestingly, neither of these assumptions has yet been verified against the actual solvents in question, which means that the real-world performance of the extraction could differ from the predicted value, either favourably or unfavourably. Overall, the results paint a promising picture, while also highlighting the importance of experimental validation going forward. In practical terms, a distribution coefficient only slightly above unity means that each individual stage achieves a relatively modest enrichment, so the burden of the separation falls heavily on the number of stages provided, and the countercurrent arrangement is what allows those stages to be used to their full cumulative effect. Before the design can be regarded as firm, laboratory or pilot work on the real solvent pair would clearly be desirable.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent in 8 countercurrent stages. The distribution coefficient is 1.02 at 25 °C; the coefficient is the ratio of the acetic acid concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase at equilibrium. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. A coefficient close to unity gives a modest enrichment per stage, and the stage count carries the separation: each countercurrent stage brings the two streams toward equilibrium at the local compositions, the extract leaves richest in acetic acid, and the raffinate leaves the last stage at the lowest acetic acid content. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages, so every stage is credited with the full transfer that equilibrium at its compositions allows. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so the solvent is treated as staying in the organic stream and the aqueous stream as leaving free of solvent. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Mutual solubility, where it occurs, moves solvent into the raffinate and water into the extract, and a stage that falls short of equilibrium transfers less acetic acid than the prediction credits to it. Predicted recovery is a design figure under two unchecked assumptions, and the check on the actual solvents is the measurement that would move it. The stage count and the coefficient together set the design: with the coefficient near unity, recovery is bought with stages, and a solvent with a higher coefficient would reach the same recovery in fewer stages, or a higher recovery in the same cascade. The raffinate is the stream the recovery figure is read on, since the figure states what the raffinate no longer carries.
